title: Bar charts that read well
summary: Bars compare things: wards, shops, teams. Sort them so the biggest is easy to find, turn them sideways with barh() when the names are long, and keep the bars starting at zero so their lengths tell the truth.
objectives: Sort a table with sort_values() before charting it.
Explain why a bar chart’s axis starts at zero.
Pick one colour for every bar.

slides.h: By the end: the wards, biggest first
slides.say: wards.csv has one row per ward of Sundarpur: population, area, parks, trees, schools and air quality. In file order, finding the biggest ward means reading every bar. Sorted, it is the first one.
points: `df = df.sort_values("Population", ascending=False)` puts the biggest first.
Months, ages and dates keep their own order: don’t sort those.
p: wards.csv has one row per ward of Sundarpur: population, area, parks, trees, schools and air quality. In file order, finding the biggest ward means reading every bar. Sorted, it is the first one.
`df = df.sort_values("Population", ascending=False)` puts the biggest first.
Months, ages and dates keep their own order: don’t sort those.

visual.what: File order: the reader hunts for the biggest.

terms: gives the table back in order of one column

slides.say: Ten ward names squash and overlap under upright bars. `plt.barh(names, values)` draws them across instead, with room for every name. barh draws the first row at the **bottom**, so sort smallest first to put the biggest on top.
points: `plt.barh(y, width)`: names up the side, lengths across.
Sort ascending (the default) for biggest at the top.

slides.say: A bar’s length is its value. Cut the axis at 90 and a ward with AQI 95 looks twice as polluted as one with 92. matplotlib starts bars at zero by itself; don’t undo it with ylim.
points: Line charts may zoom in; bar charts may not.

slides.say: Every bar is the same kind of thing, so give them one colour: `color="tab:blue"` or any colour name. A rainbow of bars makes readers look for a meaning that isn’t there. Module 4 uses colour on purpose, to pick one bar out.

quiz.code:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
df = pd.read_csv("wards.csv")
df = df.sort_values("Area_km2", ascending=False)
print(df["Ward"].tolist()[0])

bank.q: `df.sort_values("Parks")` on its own line, then a chart of df, gives…
options: bars in file order: the sorted table wasn’t kept

bank.q: A rainbow of colours on one set of bars…
options: makes readers look for a meaning that isn’t there
bank.explain: One kind of thing, one colour.

options: Tilts the names under the bars so they fit

points: Sort first: `df = df.sort_values("Col", ascending=False)`; keep natural orders (months) as they are.
`plt.barh(names, values)` for long names; sort smallest first to put the biggest on top.
Bars start at zero so their lengths tell the truth.
One colour for one kind of thing: `color="teal"`.
recap.cheat: df = df.sort_values("Col", ascending=False) · plt.barh(x, y) · color="teal"
